The @Rest(messages) annotation identifies the location of the resource bundle for a @Rest-annotated class if it's different from the class name. By default, the resource bundle name is assumed to match the class name. For example, given the class MyClass.java, the resource bundle is assumed to be MyClass.properties. This property allows you to override this setting to specify a different location such as MyMessages.properties by specifying a value of MyMessages. Resource bundles are searched using the following base name patterns: {package}.{name} {package}.i18n.{name} {package}.nls.{name} {package}.messages.{name} This annotation is used to provide request-localized (based on Accept-Language) messages for the following method: RestRequestgetMessage(String,Object) Request-localized messages are also available by passing either of the following args into your Java method: ResourceBundle - Basic Java resource bundle.Messages - Extended resource bundle with several convenience methods. The value can be a relative path like nls/Messages, indicating to look for the resource bundle com.foo.sample.nls.Messages if the resource class is in com.foo.sample, or it can be an absolute path like com.foo.sample.nls.Messages. Examples #-------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Contents of org/apache/foo/nls/MyMessages.properties #-------------------------------------------------------------------------------- HelloMessage = Hello {0}! // Contents of org/apache/foo/MyResource.java @Rest(messages="nls/MyMessages") public class MyResource { @RestGet("/hello/{you}") public Object helloYou(RestRequest req, Messages messages, @Path("name") String you) { String msg; // Get it from the RestRequest object. msg = req.getMessage("HelloMessage", you); // Or get it from the method parameter. msg = messages.getString("HelloMessage", you); // Or get the message in a locale different from the request. msg = messages.forLocale(Locale.UK).getString("HelloMessage", you); return msg; } } When using shared resource bundles, keys can be prefixed by class names like so and still retrieve by simple key names: #-------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Contents of shared org/apache/foo/nls/MyMessages.properties #-------------------------------------------------------------------------------- MyResource.HelloMessage = Hello {0}! Messages are automatically inherited from super classes. If a string cannot be found in the bundle of the current class, it will be searched for up the class hierarchy.
The REST API uses Java logging by default. If you wish to use LOG4J logging, you simple need to add the following to your JVM arguments and maven dependencies:
-Djava.util.logging.manager=org.apache.logging.log4j.jul.LogManager
<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.logging.log4j</groupId> <artifactId>log4j-jul</artifactId> </dependency>

Migration The dedicated $IF{}/$SW{}/$CO{}/$PM{}/$NE{}/$UC{}/$LC{} variable classes described in earlier versions of this page (IfVar, SwitchVar, CoalesceVar, PatternMatchVar, NotEmptyVar, UpperCaseVar, LowerCaseVar) were removed in the 10.0.0 cycle. They were replaced by a unified #{name(args...)} function-call syntax backed by org.apache.juneau.commons.svl.functions.ConditionalFunctions (if/switch/coalesce/notEmpty) and org.apache.juneau.commons.svl.functions.StringFunctions (upper/lower). See Simple Variable Language for the full, current function catalog and syntax — this page shows the config-file equivalents of the old $IF/$SW/$CO/$PM examples using the current syntax. Config files can use the #{...} function-call syntax anywhere a $Var{...} variable is valid, including nested inside other variables such as $S{...} (system property lookup). The #{if(cond,then,else)} function can be used for simple if/else logic. Unlike the old $IF{} variable, the else argument is required (pass an empty string if no "else" value is needed): # Value set to 'foo' if myBooleanProperty is true, empty otherwise. key1 = #{if($S{myBooleanProperty}, foo, "")} # Value set to 'foo' if myBooleanProperty is true, 'bar' if false. key2 = #{if($S{myBooleanProperty}, foo, bar)} # Value set to key1 value if myBooleanProperty is true, key2 value if false. key3 = #{if($S{myBooleanProperty}, $C{key1}, $C{key2})} The #{switch(...)} function can be used for switch blocks based on pattern matching. Arguments are flat and comma-delimited: value, pattern1, result1, pattern2, result2, ..., default. Patterns support */? glob wildcards (matched against the whole value): # Shell command depends on the OS shellCommand = #{switch(#{lower($S{os.name})}, *win*, bat, linux, bash, sh)} The #{coalesce(...)} function can be used for coalescing of values (finding the first non-null/empty match): # Debug flag can be enabled by system property or environment variable. debug = #{coalesce($S{debug}, $E{DEBUG}, false)} The #{match(s,regex)} function is the direct replacement for the old $PM{arg,pattern} pattern-match variable, returning "true"/"false": # Debug flag can be enabled by system property or environment variable. isWindows = #{match(#{lower($S{os.name})}, .*win.*)} See Also Simple Variable Language — the canonical reference for the full #{name(args...)} function catalog (string, type-conversion, arithmetic, boolean, conditional, regex, encoding, date/time, random/UUID, and JSON-navigation functions), plus the $Var{...} syntax these functions compose with.

See also: Health / Readiness / Liveness Probes — the health half of the management surface, and REST Server — Mixins and Multi-Mount Paths — the @Rest(mixins=...) composition primitives this page builds on. Starting with 10.0.0, Juneau ships a coherent, discoverable Actuator-style management surface while preserving Juneau's a-la-carte composability. Every endpoint exists in two independently-mountable flavors — a composable *Mixin and a routed *Resource — sharing one worker, and a convenience BasicActuatorGroup assembles them under a single configurable path prefix.

Endpoint What it does Module Default exposure GET /info Application manifest / build / version / git metadata juneau-microservice on GET /loggers, GET /loggers/{name} Read logger levels (JUL default; Logback/Log4j2 opt-in) juneau-rest-server on PUT/POST /loggers/{name} Set a logger level at runtime juneau-rest-server deny-by-default GET /metrics Prometheus scrape from a Micrometer registry juneau-rest-server-metrics-micrometer on (501 if no registry) GET /healthz, /readyz, /livez Health / readiness / liveness probes juneau-rest-server on GET /threaddump ThreadMXBean thread dump juneau-rest-server deny-by-default GET /heapdump HotSpot .hprof heap dump juneau-rest-server deny-by-default Endpoints are split across modules by dependency: /loggers (JUL backend) and the JDK-only /threaddump//heapdump need only the REST server; non-JUL /loggers backends (Logback/Log4j2) need juneau-rest-server-management-logging; /metrics needs Micrometer; /info needs the microservice runtime that resolves the application ManifestFile.

import org.apache.juneau.microservice.management.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; // Mount the whole surface under /actuator. @Rest(children=BasicActuatorGroup.class) public class RootResources extends BasicRestServletGroup { /* ... */ } BasicActuatorGroup composes InfoMixin, LoggersMixin, HealthMixin, and DumpsMixin under a single prefix. The prefix defaults to /actuator and is configurable via the juneau.actuator.path system property (resolved through the standard $S{...} SVL var): java -Djuneau.actuator.path=/manage -jar myapp.jar /metrics is not assembled into the group — it lives in the juneau-rest-server-metrics-micrometer module (which juneau-microservice does not depend on). Add MetricsMixin a-la-carte to your host resource when that module is on the classpath. Composition is convenience, not the only way in — every endpoint remains independently mountable a-la-carte via its standalone *Mixin/*Resource flavor.

The surface is on-by-default-with-gating: non-sensitive reads are exposed; mutating/sensitive operations are deny-by-default and require an explicit opt-in bean. No auth provider is auto-wired (explicit-over-magic) — wire your own guard (e.g. a BearerTokenGuard) on top. There are two complementary layers: Functional gate (deny-by-default): a settings bean (LoggersSettings, DumpsSettings) controls whether the sensitive capability is enabled at all. Off until you opt in. Authz gate (who may call it): apply a guard to the sensitive mixin at composition time with @Rest(mixinDefs=@Mixin(type=..., guards=...)) — the host-side override from Mixin Sub-Contexts. For example, to require AdminGuard on the diagnostic dumps: import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.management.*; @Rest(mixinDefs=@Mixin(type=DumpsMixin.class, guards=AdminGuard.class)) public class MyManagedResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } This guards the dump endpoints without subclassing DumpsMixin or editing it. Combine the two layers: DumpsSettings enables the dumps, @Mixin(guards=...) restricts who can call them.

The read endpoints are always on; the PUT/POST set-level endpoints respond 403 unless a LoggersSettings bean enables writes: import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.management.*; @Bean LoggersSettings loggersSettings() { return LoggersSettings.create().enableWrite().build(); }

Both diagnostics respond 403 unless a DumpsSettings bean opts them in (independently). /heapdump additionally responds 501 on a JVM without HotSpot heap-dump support, and streams a self-deleting .hprof temp file when enabled: @Bean DumpsSettings dumpsSettings() { return DumpsSettings.create() .enableThreadDump() .enableHeapDump() .build(); } Why deny-by-default? A thread dump can leak sensitive runtime state; a heap dump can be large and contain secrets. Both stay off until an operator explicitly opts in.

/info renders the running application's META-INF/MANIFEST.MF main attributes — sourced from Microservice.getManifest() — as a JSON map. With no manifest registered it degrades cleanly to {}. To surface build/version/git metadata, stamp them into your application jar's manifest at build time. /info reads your app jar's manifest, so the stamping goes in your build, not Juneau's. A typical Maven recipe: <!-- 1. Capture git metadata into Maven properties. --> <plugin> <groupId>io.github.git-commit-id</groupId> <artifactId>git-commit-id-maven-plugin</artifactId> <executions> <execution><goals><goal>revision</goal></goals></execution> </executions> <configuration> <generateGitPropertiesFile>false</generateGitPropertiesFile> </configuration> </plugin> <!-- 2. Stamp them (plus version/build-time) into MANIFEST.MF. --> <plugin> <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId> <artifactId>maven-jar-plugin</artifactId> <configuration> <archive> <manifest> <addDefaultImplementationEntries>true</addDefaultImplementationEntries> </manifest> <manifestEntries> <Build-Time>${maven.build.timestamp}</Build-Time> <Git-Commit-Id>${git.commit.id.abbrev}</Git-Commit-Id> <Git-Branch>${git.branch}</Git-Branch> </manifestEntries> </archive> </configuration> </plugin> addDefaultImplementationEntries contributes Implementation-Title/Implementation-Version; the manifestEntries add the git/build fields. All of them then appear in /info: { "Implementation-Version": "1.4.2", "Build-Time": "2026-06-17T00:00:00Z", "Git-Commit-Id": "abc1234", "Git-Branch": "main" }

/metrics strictly consumes a consumer-provided MeterRegistry resolved from the bean store — it never auto-registers a default (consistent with micrometer-core being a provided dependency). It renders a Prometheus text scrape when a PrometheusMeterRegistry is present and degrades to 501 Not Implemented otherwise. @Bean MeterRegistry meterRegistry() { return new PrometheusMeterRegistry(PrometheusConfig.DEFAULT); } Mount the endpoint by mixing MetricsMixin into your host resource (the juneau-rest-server-metrics-micrometer module must be on the classpath).

The /loggers endpoint drives a LogBackend. By default that is java.util.logging (JulLogBackend) — the backend Juneau itself configures, and the only one bundled with juneau-rest-server (the core stays dependency-free). Applications that route logging through SLF4J→Logback or Log4j2 select the matching backend explicitly.

Consistent with Juneau's explicit-over-magic stance, you declare the backend on a LoggersSettings bean — the endpoint never classpath-scans for, and then silently drives, a backend you didn't choose. The Logback / Log4j2 adapters ship in the opt-in juneau-rest-server-management-logging module (the backends are declared provided, so they never leak transitively onto your classpath): <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-management-logging</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- plus your chosen backend at the version you want, e.g. ch.qos.logback:logback-classic --> @Bean public LoggersSettings loggersSettings() { return LoggersSettings.create() .enableWrite() // opt in to the set-level endpoints (deny-by-default) .backend(new LogbackLogBackend()) // or new Log4j2LogBackend() — explicit, no auto-detect .build(); } When no LoggersSettings bean is registered (or none declares a backend), the endpoint drives JUL.

The endpoint's contract is identical regardless of backend: Read reports each logger's configured level — the level set on the logger itself, or the empty string when it inherits from an ancestor (Log4j2 LoggerConfigs always carry a concrete level, so the empty-string "inherited" marker only appears for JUL/Logback). The root logger is keyed ROOT. Set is process-lifetime-only (JUL Logger.setLevel, Logback Logger.setLevel, Log4j2 Configurator.setLevel) — it does not rewrite the backend's configuration file. A blank/empty level clears the logger's own level so it inherits again. Level names are backend-native (JUL FINE/INFO/…; Logback & Log4j2 DEBUG/INFO/WARN/…). An invalid level name fails with 400.

SLF4J itself emits nothing; the levels live in the bound backend. Select the backend that actually emits: LogbackLogBackend for SLF4J→Logback, Log4j2LogBackend for Log4j2 (including SLF4J→Log4j2). When the SLF4J binding is slf4j-jdk14 (SLF4J→JUL), the backend is JUL, so the default JulLogBackend is correct. Custom backends can implement LogBackend directly.
documents.s: SLF4J is a facade — pick the real backend

documents.t: The Microservice.Builder.manifest(Object) method can be used to specify the contents or location of of the main manifest file of the executable jar. If you do not specify the location/contents of the manifest file, the microservice will attempt to resolve it through the following methods: - Looking on the file system for a file at META-INF/MANIFEST.MF. This is primarily to allow for running microservices from within eclipse workspaces where the manifest file is located in the project root. Using the class loader for this class to find the file at the URL META-INF/MANIFEST.MF. If you do manually specify the manifest file, you can pass in any of the following types: Manifest File TypesManifestFile - A pre-parsed manifest fileManifest - A pre-parsed manifest fileReader - Containing the raw contents of the manifestInputStream - Containing the raw contents of the manifestFile - File containing the raw contents of the manifestString - Path to file containing the raw contents of the manifestClass - Finds and loads the manifest file of the jar file that the specified class is contained within The manifest file can be retrieved using the the Microservice.getManifest() method which provides an API for accessing manifest file entries. This method returns an instance of ManifestFile — a lean, immutable wrapper around a java.util.jar.Manifest that returns Optional<String> from its get(...) accessors. Example ManifestFile manifestFile = Microservice.getInstance().getManifest(); String mainClass = manifestFile.get("Main-Class").orElse(null); int myInt = manifestFile.get("My-Int").map(Integer::parseInt).orElse(123); boolean myBoolean = manifestFile.get("My-Boolean").map(Boolean::parseBoolean).orElse(false); The manifest is also used for the $MF SVL variable. Examples // $MF used in variable resolver. VarResolver var = Microservice.getInstance().getVarResolver(); System.out.println(var.resolve("The main class is $MF{Main-Class}")); // $MF used in annotation. @Rest( title="$MF{Application-Title}", ... )

The org.apache.juneau.marshall.markdown package provides Markdown serialization and parsing for POJOs. Output is optimized for human readability and LLM/AI consumption. Markdown support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>
Mode Serializer Use Case Fragment MarkdownSerializer Compact tables/lists for embedding Document MarkdownDocSerializer Full documents with headings for nested structure

Input type Markdown output Single Bean 2-column key-value table Single Map 2-column key-value table Collection<Bean> Multi-column table with header row Collection<Map> Multi-column table with header row Collection<SimpleType> Bulleted list Nested bean (in table cell) Inline JSON5 in backticks

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Fragment mode - table output List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); String md = MarkdownSerializer.DEFAULT.write(people); // Produces: // | name | age | // |------|-----| // | Alice | 30 | // | Bob | 25 | // Document mode - with headings String doc = MarkdownDocSerializer.create().title("Report").build().write(people); // Use the marshaller String md2 = Markdown.of(people); List<Person> parsed = Markdown.to(md, List.class, Person.class);

Document mode uses headings for nested structure: public class Person { public String name; public Address address; } MarkdownDocSerializer s = MarkdownDocSerializer.create().title("Person").build(); String md = s.write(person); Produces: # Person | Property | Value | |----------|-------| | name | John | ## address | Property | Value | |----------|-------| | city | Springfield | | state | IL |

Each mode has its own marshaller — a serializer/parser pairing with convenience of(...) / to(...) methods: Marshaller Backing serializer/parser Output Markdown MarkdownSerializer / MarkdownParser Fragment — a bare table or list, ideal for embedding inside a larger document MarkdownDoc MarkdownDocSerializer / MarkdownDocParser Document — a full Markdown document that uses headings (#, ##, …) to represent nested structure Use Markdown when the result will be spliced into another document (for example, a table inside an LLM prompt or a README). Use MarkdownDoc when you want a standalone document whose nesting is expressed as a heading hierarchy rather than inline JSON5. List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); // Fragment marshaller - just the table String fragment = Markdown.DEFAULT.of(people); // Document marshaller - full document with headings String document = MarkdownDoc.DEFAULT.of(people); // Both round-trip back to POJOs List<Person> parsed = MarkdownDoc.DEFAULT.to(document, List.class, Person.class);

For one-off conversions without holding a marshaller reference, MarshallUtils provides static shortcuts that delegate to the Markdown.DEFAULT and MarkdownDoc.DEFAULT instances: Method Delegates to Purpose markdown(Object) Markdown.DEFAULT.of(...) Serialize to a fragment markdown(Object, Class) Markdown.DEFAULT.to(...) Parse a fragment into a POJO markdownDoc(Object) MarkdownDoc.DEFAULT.of(...) Serialize to a whole document markdownDoc(Object, Class) MarkdownDoc.DEFAULT.to(...) Parse a whole document into a POJO import static org.apache.juneau.marshall.marshaller.MarshallUtils.*; String fragment = markdown(people); // fragment mode String document = markdownDoc(people); // document mode
Produces: text/markdown Accepts: text/markdown, text/x-markdown
// Markdown is included in BasicUniversalConfig @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... }
Markdown package Javadoc

The org.apache.juneau.marshall.encoders package defines an API for handling encoding-based matching of Accept-Encoding/Content-Encoding HTTP headers. It consists of the following classes: EncoderSetEncoderIdentityEncoderGzipEncoder

The EncoderSet class represents the set of Encoders keyed by codings. It maintains a set of encoders and the codings that they can handle. The getEncoderMatch(String) and EncoderSet.getEncoder(String) methods are then used to find appropriate encoders for specific Accept-Encoding and Content-Encoding header values.

Encoders are tried in the order they appear in the set. The EncoderSet.Builder.add(Class...) / EncoderSet.Builder.add(Encoder...) methods prepend the values to the list to allow them the opportunity to override encoders already in the list. For example, calling builder.add(E1.class,E2.class).add(E3.class, E4.class) will result in the order E3, E4, E1, E2. Example // Create an encoder group with support for gzip compression. EncoderSet encoders = EncoderSet .create() .add(GzipEncoder.class) .build(); // Get the encoder for "gzip" Encoder encoder = encoders.getEncoder("compress;q=1.0, gzip;q=0.8, identity;q=0.5, *;q=0");

The Encoder interface is used for enabling decompression on requests and compression on responses, such as support for GZIP compression. It is used to wrap input and output streams within compression/decompression streams. EncodergetCodings()getInputStream(InputStream)getOutputStream(OutputStream) note Encoders are registered with RestServlets through the @Rest(encoders) annotation.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.svl package defines "Simple Variable Language" (SVL) — text containing variables of the form $varName{varKey} that are resolved by a VarResolver. SVL is used extensively across the Config, REST, and Microservice APIs, and by many Juneau annotations so that values can be sourced from configuration files, environment variables, and system properties. The canonical reference for the language itself — the built-in source variables, the #{...} function-call syntax and function catalog, the VarTemplate compiled-template API, and Supplier<String> live-reload patterns — is Simple Variable Language. This section collects the marshall-context-specific SVL topics: SVL Variables — the variables available in a REST context. VarResolvers — creating and configuring resolvers. VarResolver.DEFAULT — the reusable default resolver. SVL Other Notes — escaping, recursion, and efficiency notes. // The default resolver handles $S (system property) and $E (environment) variables out of the box. String property = VarResolver.DEFAULT.resolve("The Java home directory is $S{java.home}");

Simple Variable Language — the full SVL language reference. @Value Annotation Basics — declarative config injection built on SVL. @Value Framework-Internal Adoption org.apache.juneau.commons.svl.VarResolver

The @Marshalled annotation is a class-level annotation in org.apache.juneau.marshall that controls how a class is serialized and parsed across all Juneau marshalling formats (JSON, XML, HTML, MessagePack, and the rest). It is the format-side counterpart to @BeanType. @Marshalled carries the marshalling-only attributes — marshalling strategy, type naming, bean dictionary, implementation class, interceptors, POJO examples, and wire-format overrides — while the bean-modeling attributes (properties, excludeProperties, findFluentSetters, interfaceClass, stopClass, propertyNamer, unsorted, ...) live on @BeanType in juneau-commons. @Marshalled(typeName="address") public class Address { public String street; public String city; } Migration Prior to the 10.0 refactor, the bean-modeling members now on @BeanType were part of @Marshalled. @Marshalled retains only the marshalling-layer attributes documented below; see @BeanType Annotation for the model side.

@Marshalled participates transparently in every marshaller. Here the example attribute supplies a canonical POJO example, and the type round-trips through JSON5: @Marshalled(example="{street:'123 Main St',city:'Springfield'}") public class Address { public String street; public String city; } Address a = new Address(); a.street = "123 Main St"; a.city = "Springfield"; // Serialize. String json = Json5.DEFAULT.of(a); // {street:'123 Main St',city:'Springfield'} // Parse back. Address a2 = Json5.DEFAULT.to(json, Address.class);

The @Marshalled(as) attribute selects the marshalling strategy from the MarshalledAs enum. The default is MarshalledAs.DETECT (auto-detection). Use MarshalledAs.STRING to serialize via toString() and parse via a fromString/valueOf/single-String constructor — the declarative replacement for the old MarshallingStringSwap pattern. // Serialize/parse this type as a single string value. @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.STRING) public class PhoneNumber { private final String value; public PhoneNumber(String value) { this.value = value; } // single-String constructor for parsing @Override public String toString() { return value; } // used for serialization } See @MarshalledAs Enum for full details.

typeName assigns a dictionary name to a class so the serializer can emit a type discriminator when the static type is ambiguous (for example, a property declared as Object), and the parser can resolve the concrete class from that name. typePropertyName overrides the property used to hold the discriminator (default _type). @Marshalled(typeName="cat") public class Cat extends Animal {} @Marshalled(typeName="dog", typePropertyName="kind") public class Dog extends Animal {} When a Cat is serialized through a property of the base Animal type, the output includes _type:'cat' so it can be parsed back to the correct subclass. See Bean Dictionaries for how type names are registered and resolved.

The @Marshalled(dictionary) attribute registers the set of classes that make up the bean dictionary for all properties in this class and its subclasses. Combined with typeName, this lets polymorphic properties round-trip. @Marshalled(dictionary={Cat.class, Dog.class}) public class Pet { public Animal animal; // resolved to Cat or Dog via _type on parse } The dictionary can also be registered globally on the marshalling context: WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer .create() .beanDictionary(Cat.class, Dog.class) .build(); See Bean Sub Types for a worked subtype example.

For interfaces and abstract classes, @Marshalled(implClass) specifies the concrete class to instantiate during parsing. @Marshalled(implClass=MyInterfaceImpl.class) public interface MyInterface { ... }

The @Marshalled(interceptor) attribute registers a BeanInterceptor that can transform property values in transit — rewriting values on read (serialize) and write (parse). // Redact a sensitive property on serialization. public class AddressInterceptor extends BeanInterceptor<Address> { @Override public Object readProperty(Address bean, String name, Object value) { return "taxInfo".equals(name) ? "redacted" : value; } } @Marshalled(interceptor=AddressInterceptor.class) public class Address { public String getTaxInfo() { ... } public void setTaxInfo(String value) { ... } }

The @Marshalled(example) attribute supplies an example instance of the class in JSON5 (Simplified JSON) format. Examples are surfaced in generated Swagger/OpenAPI documents. The value supports VarResolver.DEFAULT substitution (e.g. $C{myConfigVar}). @Marshalled(example="{foo:'bar',baz:123}") public class MyClass { ... } The same example can be defined in code with the @Example annotation on a static field or method — see @Example Annotation.

@Marshalled can override the default wire format for common datatypes on a per-class basis. Each override defaults to NOT_SET (inherit the context default). The available attributes are: Attribute Applies to Enum calendarFormat Calendar CalendarFormat dateFormat Date DateFormat durationFormat Duration DurationFormat temporalFormat java.time.* TemporalFormat localeFormat Locale LocaleFormat timeZoneFormat TimeZone TimeZoneFormat binaryFormat byte[] BinaryFormat enumFormat enums EnumFormat uuidFormat UUID UuidFormat bitSetFormat BitSet BitSetFormat bigNumberFormat BigInteger / BigDecimal BigNumberFormat booleanFormat Boolean / boolean BooleanFormat floatFormat Float / Double (non-finite) FloatFormat currencyFormat Currency CurrencyFormat classFormat Class ClassFormat periodFormat Period PeriodFormat // Serialize byte[] values as hex and enums as lower-hyphenated names for this class. @Marshalled(binaryFormat=BinaryFormat.HEX, enumFormat=EnumFormat.LOWER_HYPHEN) public class MyBean { public byte[] data; public MyEnum status; }

The same attributes can be applied in bulk to third-party classes without annotating them directly, using @MarshalledConfig (with on/onClass) on @Rest-annotated classes and @RestOp-annotated methods via @MarshalledApply. See Also @BeanType Annotation - The model-side annotation in juneau-commons. @MarshalledAs Enum - The marshalling strategy used by as. @MarshalledFilter Annotation - The runtime/programmatic equivalent of @Marshalled. @Example Annotation - Defining POJO examples in code. Bean Dictionaries - Type names and polymorphic marshalling. Marshallers - The marshaller API overview. The Java doclink docs/topics/MarshalledAnnotation on Marshalled.java resolves to this page.
documents.s: Applying to REST Classes and Methods

documents.t: MarshalledAs is an enum in org.apache.juneau.marshall that specifies the marshalling strategy for a type annotated with @Marshalled. It is the value type of the @Marshalled(as) attribute.

Value Behavior DETECT Auto-detect the strategy (default). The marshalling engine inspects the type and picks the best representation — bean, map, collection, string swap, and so on. STRING Serialize using Object.toString() and parse using a fromString(String), valueOf(String), or single-String-argument constructor.

DETECT is the default when as is not specified. It lets Juneau choose how to represent the type based on reflection — most classes are modeled as beans, Map/Collection types as objects/arrays, and types with a recognized string transform as strings. You rarely need to set this explicitly. // Equivalent to no 'as' attribute at all. @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.DETECT) public class MyBean { public String name; public int age; }

MarshalledAs.STRING marshals the whole object as a single string. On serialize, Juneau calls toString(); on parse, it reconstructs the object from a fromString(String) static method, a valueOf(String) static method, or a single-String constructor. This is the declarative replacement for the former MarshallingStringSwap pattern — no separate swap class is required. @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.STRING) public class PhoneNumber { private final String value; // Single-String constructor used for parsing. public PhoneNumber(String value) { this.value = value; } // Used for serialization. @Override public String toString() { return value; } } Serialize / parse round-trip: PhoneNumber p = new PhoneNumber("555-1234"); // Serializes to the toString() value: "555-1234" String json = Json5.DEFAULT.of(p); // Parses back via the single-String constructor. PhoneNumber p2 = Json5.DEFAULT.to(json, PhoneNumber.class); Because the object collapses to a single scalar, it appears inline wherever it is used — for example as a map key or a quoted value — rather than as a nested object. Migration Applying @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.STRING) to a class reproduces the pre-9.5 behavior in which @BeanIgnore on a class caused toString() serialization. See @MarshalledIgnore Annotation for the current @MarshalledIgnore semantics (which instead output null). See Also @Marshalled Annotation - The class-level annotation that uses this enum. Swaps - The general-purpose object-transform mechanism for finer control.

MarshalledFilter is the class in org.apache.juneau.marshall that customizes how a POJO or bean is handled during serialization and parsing. It is the programmatic, runtime equivalent of the @Marshalled and @BeanType annotations combined — it is the single concrete BeanFilter implementation in the framework. In normal use you never construct a MarshalledFilter yourself. When Juneau analyzes a class it reads the @Marshalled and @BeanType annotations (plus any config-level overrides) and builds a MarshalledFilter internally — this is what ClassMeta and MarshalledBeanMetaInitializer do behind the scenes. The filter is then consulted for every property during marshalling.

A MarshalledFilter captures both the format-side (@Marshalled) and model-side (@BeanType) decisions for a class: Filter attribute Annotation source Purpose properties @BeanType(properties) Property inclusion and ordering. excludeProperties @BeanType(excludeProperties) Properties to omit. readOnlyProperties @BeanType(readOnlyProperties) Serialized but not parsed. writeOnlyProperties @BeanType(writeOnlyProperties) Parsed but not serialized. propertyNamer @BeanType(propertyNamer) Property-name transformation. interfaceClass @BeanType(interfaceClass) Limit properties to an interface. stopClass @BeanType(stopClass) Halt hierarchy traversal. unsortedProperties @BeanType(unsorted) Opt out of alphabetical sorting. fluentSetters @BeanType(findFluentSetters) Detect fluent setters. typeName @Marshalled(typeName) Bean dictionary type name. dictionary @Marshalled(dictionary) Bean dictionary classes. implClass @Marshalled(implClass) Concrete class for an interface/abstract type. interceptor @Marshalled(interceptor) Getter/setter interceptor. example @Marshalled(example) POJO example value.

For advanced or dynamic scenarios you can build a filter directly with MarshalledFilter.create(...), which returns a Builder. The builder mirrors the annotation attributes: MarshalledFilter filter = MarshalledFilter .create(ClassInfo.of(Address.class)) .properties("id,name,email") // include only these, in this order .excludeProperties("password") // never serialize sensitive data .readOnlyProperties("id") // id is serialized but ignored on parse .typeName("address") // dictionary name .unsortedProperties() // keep declared order .build(); The builder also has two apply methods used by the framework to fold annotations into a filter: applyAnnotations(List<Marshalled>) — applies the marshalling-side attributes (typeName, interceptor, implClass, dictionary, example). applyBeanTypeAnnotations(List<BeanType>) — applies the bean-modeling attributes (properties, excludeProperties, readOnly/writeOnly, propertyNamer, interfaceClass, stopClass, unsorted, findFluentSetters).

Once built, a MarshalledFilter exposes read-only getters (getProperties(), getExcludeProperties(), getExample(), getTypeName(), getImplClass(), getInterfaceClass(), getStopClass(), getBeanDictionary(), ...) that the serializer and parser query. It also implements the interceptor hooks readProperty(bean, name, value) (on serialize) and writeProperty(bean, name, value) (on parse), delegating to the configured BeanInterceptor. note Because a filter is derived from @Marshalled and @BeanType, the recommended way to customize a class is to declare those annotations (or their config-level equivalents) rather than building filters by hand. Reach for MarshalledFilter.create(...) only when the class cannot be annotated or the configuration must be computed at runtime. See Also @Marshalled Annotation - The declarative, format-side equivalent. @BeanType Annotation - The declarative, model-side equivalent. Marshallers - The marshaller API overview.

The MarshalledNode class is a typed tree façade layered over the generic-collections model — MarshalledMap / MarshalledList and their JsonMap / JsonList subclasses. It gives developers coming from Jackson the ergonomics they expect — node-type introspection, typed value accessors, fluent tree building, and RFC 6901 JSON-Pointer addressing — without introducing a parallel Jackson-style node hierarchy. important MarshalledNode is a live view, not a copy and not a new node type. A node wraps a single backing value that is one of: a Map (an object node), a List (an array node), a scalar (String, Number, Boolean, …) (a value node), or null (a null node). The underlying representation is still plain MarshalledMap/MarshalledList (or any Map/List). There is no ObjectNode / ArrayNode / TextNode class tree to learn — MarshalledNode is the single façade type for every node kind.

Use the static factories to wrap an existing value or to start a fresh tree: // Wrap an existing value (stored as-is, no copy). MarshalledNode node = MarshalledNode.of(myJsonMap); // Start fresh containers (backed by a new empty JsonMap / JsonList). MarshalledNode obj = MarshalledNode.objectNode(); MarshalledNode arr = MarshalledNode.arrayNode(); You can also obtain a node directly from the collections classes via the convenience MarshalledMap.at(String) and MarshalledList.at(String) methods, which resolve an RFC 6901 pointer and return a MarshalledNode: JsonMap doc = Json.to("{foo:{bar:['x','y']}}", JsonMap.class); // Returns a MarshalledNode wrapping "y". MarshalledNode n = doc.at("/foo/bar/1");
Four predicates report the kind of value a node wraps: isObject() — wraps a Map.isArray() — wraps a List.isValue() — wraps a non-null scalar.isNull() — wraps null.

Value nodes can be read in a target type. The scalar accessors return null when the node is not a value node or the value cannot be converted (rather than throwing): String s = node.get("name").asString(); Integer i = node.get("age").asInt(); Long l = node.get("id").asLong(); Double d = node.get("score").asDouble(); Boolean b = node.get("active").asBoolean(); For richer conversions — including converting an object node straight to a bean — use as(Class), which routes through the same conversion machinery as MarshalledMap.get(String,Class). Use value() to get the raw backing object: // Convert an object node to a bean. Address addr = node.get("address").as(Address.class); // Get the raw backing value. Object raw = node.value();

Navigate into children by key (object nodes) or index (array nodes). Both get(...) forms return null on a miss (absent key, out-of-range index, or wrong node kind), and size() returns the entry/element count (0 for value and null nodes): MarshalledNode child = node.get("address"); // by key MarshalledNode first = node.get("phones").get(0); // by index int count = node.get("phones").size();

The put(String,Object) (object nodes) and add(Object) (array nodes) builders return this for chaining. They mutate the backing container in place, so callers still holding the underlying map/list see the change. Example // Build a tree fluently (mutates a backing JsonMap/JsonList in place). MarshalledNode node = MarshalledNode.objectNode() .put("a", 1) .put("b", MarshalledNode.arrayNode().add("x").add("y").value()); String json = Json.of(node.value()); // {"a":1,"b":["x","y"]} // Navigate and read typed values. Integer a = node.get("a").asInt(); // 1 String x = node.get("b").get(0).asString(); // "x" put(...) on a non-object node and add(...) on a non-array node both throw IllegalStateException.

Because a node is a live view, building or mutating through it changes the shared backing container: JsonMap backing = new JsonMap(); MarshalledNode node = MarshalledNode.of(backing); node.put("x", 1); // backing now contains {"x":1} — the caller's map saw the mutation. When you need an independent snapshot, use copy(), which returns a new node backed by a recursive deep copy (maps into new JsonMaps, lists into new JsonLists; scalars and null are returned as-is). Mutating the copy never affects the original and vice versa: MarshalledNode snapshot = node.copy(); snapshot.put("x", 999); // does not affect the original 'node'.

MarshalledNode exposes the full RFC 6901 pointer surface relative to its backing value: at(String) — read; returns the addressed node or null on a read-miss.find(String) — read returning an Optional<MarshalledNode> (distinguishes a present null value from an absent one).set(String,Object) — auto-vivifying write; the - token appends to a list. The root pointer is rejected.remove(String) — removes the addressed member/element and returns it (null if absent). JsonMap doc = Json.to("{foo:{bar:['x','y']}}", JsonMap.class); MarshalledNode root = MarshalledNode.of(doc); // Read. String y = root.at("/foo/bar/1").asString(); // "y" // Optional read — present even when the value is JSON null. Optional<MarshalledNode> maybe = root.find("/foo/baz"); // Optional.empty() // Auto-vivifying write — intermediate containers are created as needed. root.set("/foo/qux/0", "new"); // creates {foo:{qux:["new"]}} alongside bar // Append to a list with the '-' token. root.set("/foo/bar/-", "z"); // bar is now ['x','y','z'] // Remove. Object removed = root.remove("/foo/bar/0"); // returns "x" A read-miss (missing key, out-of-range index, or type mismatch) resolves to null from at(...). The empty pointer "" addresses the whole backing document; on a node, set("", …) is rejected with IllegalArgumentException because the backing value cannot be replaced in place — set against a non-empty pointer instead.

For pointer operations against an arbitrary Map/List root (not just through a node), use the standalone JsonPointer class directly. A pointer is a string of zero or more /-prefixed reference tokens; the empty string "" references the whole document (the root), and a non-empty pointer must begin with /. JsonMap doc = JsonMap.of("foo", JsonList.of("bar", "baz")); // Read (read-miss resolves to null). Object v = JsonPointer.of("/foo/0").eval(doc); // "bar" // Auto-vivifying write; '-' appends. Returns the (possibly new) effective root. JsonPointer.of("/foo/-").set(doc, "qux"); // appends "qux" // Remove returns the removed value (null if absent). Object removed = JsonPointer.of("/foo/0").remove(doc); // "bar"

Within a reference token, / is escaped as ~1 and ~ is escaped as ~0 (decode order matters: ~1→/ first, then ~0→~). Use encodeToken(String) and decodeToken(String) to convert between raw member names and escaped tokens: // A member name literally named "a/b~c". JsonPointer.encodeToken("a/b~c"); // "a~1b~0c" JsonPointer.decodeToken("a~1b~0c"); // "a/b~c" // Addressing that member: JsonMap doc = Json.to("{'a/b~c':42}", JsonMap.class); Object v = JsonPointer.of("/a~1b~0c").eval(doc); // 42 On a write, the special - token references "the element after the last element" of an array — i.e. it appends: JsonMap doc = Json.to("{items:[1,2]}", JsonMap.class); JsonPointer.of("/items/-").set(doc, 3); // items is now [1,2,3] toString() round-trips a parsed pointer back to its canonical escaped string form. Array index tokens are strict base-10 non-negative integers with no leading zeros (0 itself is allowed); anything else is treated as an object member name. note MarshalledNode and JsonPointer are part of the next-generation typed tree model layered over the Marshalled* collections and are marked Beta — API subject to change. The underlying MarshalledMap/MarshalledList path-navigation methods (getAt/putAt/postAt/deleteAt) remain the stable, long-standing way to address nodes by slash-delimited path.

documents.t: Marshallers are simple pairings of a Serializer and Parser with convenience methods for serializing and parsing POJOs. MarshallerT to(Object,Class<T>)CharMarshallerString of(Object)Csv Hjson Hocon Html Ini Jcs Json Json5 Json5l Jsonl Markdown MarkdownDoc OpenApi PlainText Prototext Sse Toml Uon UrlEncoding Xml YamlStreamMarshallerbyte[] of(Object)Bson Cbor MsgPack Parquet Protobuf Examples // Using instance. Json json = new Json(); MyPojo myPojo = json.to(string, MyPojo.class); String string = json.of(myPojo); // Using DEFAULT instance. MyPojo myPojo = Json.DEFAULT.to(string, MyPojo.class); String string = Json.DEFAULT.of(myPojo); Juneau comes with the following predefined marshallers: BsonCborCsvHjsonHoconHtmlIniJcsJsonJson5Json5lJsonlMarkdownMarkdownDocMsgPackOpenApiParquetPlainTextProtobufPrototextSseTomlUonUrlEncodingXmlYaml Each predefined marshaller also includes static convenience from/to methods to make it even easier to perform marshalling on POJOs: JsonString of(Object)T to(Object,Class) Examples // Using shortcut static methods. MyPojo myPojo = Json.to(jsonString, MyPojo.class); String json = Json.of(myPojo);

In addition to the String / byte[] static shortcuts shown above, every marshaller facade also provides static shortcuts that read from and write to streams: Character formats (Json, Xml, Html, Yaml, Ini, Hjson, …) add: to(Reader, Class<T>) to(Reader, Type, Type...) of(Object, Writer) Binary formats (MsgPack, Cbor, Bson, Protobuf, Parquet) add: to(InputStream, Class<T>) to(InputStream, Type, Type...) of(Object, OutputStream) // Parse from a Reader / InputStream: MyPojo a = Json.to(reader, MyPojo.class); MyPojo b = MsgPack.to(inputStream, MyPojo.class); // Serialize to a Writer / OutputStream: Json.of(myPojo, writer); MsgPack.of(myPojo, outputStream); Unlike the instance read(...) / write(...) methods (which throw a checked IOException), these static shortcuts wrap any IOException from the underlying stream into an unchecked ParseException (on the to(...) read side) or SerializeException (on the of(...) serialize side), so they can be used directly in lambdas and streams without a checked-exception burden. note There are intentionally no File overloads. The core I/O surface is stream-only (see the 10.0.0 breaking-change note on narrowing serializer/parser I/O to streams). To read from or write to a file, open the Reader / Writer / InputStream / OutputStream yourself: // Serialize to a file (character format): try (Writer w = Files.newBufferedWriter(path)) { Json.of(myPojo, w); } // Parse from a file (binary format): try (InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(path)) { MyPojo p = MsgPack.to(in, MyPojo.class); }

A handful of formats ship dedicated variant facade classes for a commonly-used non-default configuration. Each variant is a subclass of its base format facade with its own DEFAULT instance and the full static shortcut surface bound to that instance: Json5R — readable (indented) JSON5, backed by Json5Serializer.DEFAULT_READABLE.IniR — readable (spaced) INI, backed by IniSerializer.DEFAULT_READABLE.HjsonC — compact (single-line) Hjson, backed by HjsonSerializer.DEFAULT_COMPACT. // Readable JSON5: String pretty = Json5R.of(myPojo); // Compact Hjson: String compact = HjsonC.of(myPojo); These replace the former Json5.DEFAULT_READABLE, Ini.DEFAULT_READABLE, and Hjson.DEFAULT_COMPACT constants (removed in 10.0.0) — a variant class is a first-class facade, so it exposes the same static of(...) / to(...) shortcut API (including the stream-based shortcuts above) as any other marshaller.

MarshallUtils provides a single set of statically-imported convenience methods that cover every serialization format. Instead of referencing a specific marshaller class, you import MarshallUtils.* and call format-named methods directly. import static org.apache.juneau.marshall.marshaller.MarshallUtils.*; // Serialize to any text format String a = json(myBean); String b = json5(myBean); String c = xml(myBean); String d = yaml(myBean); String e = toml(myBean); String f = csv(myBean); // Serialize to binary formats byte[] m = msgPack(myBean); byte[] n = cbor(myBean); byte[] o = bson(myBean); // Parse — same method name, overloaded by input MyBean b1 = json(jsonString, MyBean.class); MyBean b2 = xml(xmlString, MyBean.class); MyBean b3 = msgPack(bytes, MyBean.class);

Method Format Serialize output json(o) Standard JSON (RFC 8259) String json5(o) JSON5 String jsonl(o) JSON Lines (NDJSON) String jcs(o) Canonical JSON (RFC 8785) String hjson(o) HJSON String xml(o) XML String html(o) HTML String uon(o) URL-Encoded Object Notation String urlEncoding(o) URL Encoding String yaml(o) YAML String csv(o) CSV String openApi(o) OpenAPI String plainText(o) Plain text String markdown(o) Markdown (fragment) String markdownDoc(o) Markdown (document) String ini(o) INI / properties String toml(o) TOML String hocon(o) HOCON String proto(o) Protobuf Text Format String msgPack(o) MessagePack byte[] cbor(o) CBOR (RFC 8949) byte[] bson(o) BSON byte[] parquet(o) Apache Parquet byte[]

Every format method provides the following overloads: Signature Purpose format(Object) Serialize to String or byte[] format(Object, Object) Serialize to a Writer or OutputStream format(Object, Class<T>) Parse from any input — throws checked IOException format(Object, Type, Type...) Parse from any input with a parameterized type — throws checked IOException format(String, Class<T>) Parse from String — exceptions wrapped as unchecked format(String, Type, Type...) Parse from String with a parameterized type — unchecked format(byte[], Class<T>) Parse from byte[] (binary formats) — unchecked format(byte[], Type, Type...) Parse from byte[] with a parameterized type — unchecked The String- and byte[]-input overloads wrap ParseException / IOException in unchecked runtime exceptions so they can be used directly in lambdas and streams. // Checked overload — use when the caller can handle IOException MyBean bean = json(reader, MyBean.class); // Unchecked overload — convenient in lambdas/streams List<MyBean> beans = inputStrings.stream() .map(s -> json(s, MyBean.class)) .toList(); // Parameterized type List<MyBean> list = json(jsonString, List.class, MyBean.class); Map<String, MyBean> map = json(jsonString, Map.class, String.class, MyBean.class); // Write to an existing Writer or OutputStream json(myBean, responseWriter); msgPack(myBean, outputStream);

Outdated examples (9.5) Examples on this page using RestContext.Builder is pre-9.5 and kept only for historical context. Use @Rest(...serializers/parsers...), @RestOp(...), or @Bean(name="serializers"|"parsers") with fully built sets. See the v9.5 Migration Guide. Juneau uses Parsers and Serializers for marshalling HTTP request and response bodies to POJOs using the Content-Type header to match the best parser and the Accept header to match the best serializer. Serializers and parsers can be associated with REST servlets using the following annotations: RestserializersparsersRestOpserializersparsers Request bodies are parsed and passed in via @Content-annotated parameters, and response bodies are returned or thrown by @RestOp-annotated methods and serialized. Example @Rest( serializers={JsonParser.class, HtmlSerializer.class}, parsers={JsonParser.class, HtmlParser.class} ) public class MyResource { // Override at the method level. @RestPost(parsers={XmlParser.class}) public MyPojo myMethod(@Content MyPojo myPojo) { // Do something with your parsed POJO. // Then return it and serialize the POJO. } } The following classes provide common default serializers and parsers that can be used as-is or augmented by child classes: Classes:BasicRestServlet BasicRestServletGroup BasicRestResource BasicRestResourceGroupInterfaces:BasicJsonConfig BasicJsonHtmlConfig BasicJson5Config BasicOpenApiConfig BasicYamlConfig BasicUniversalConfig Serializers and parsers can also be supplied programmatically using @Bean bean suppliers (for example, name="serializers" and name="parsers"). They can also be defined through custom REST contexts. Config annotations allow you to define serializer and parser properties using specialized annotations at either the class or operation levels: @Rest( ... ) @MarshalledConfig(sortProperties="true") @SerializerConfig(trimNulls="true") @JsonConfig(escapeSolidus="true") public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestPost @MarshalledConfig(sortProperties="false") @SerializerConfig(trimNulls="false") public MyPojo myMethod(@Content MyPojo myPojo) { ... } } Swaps are associated serializers and parsers registered on a REST resource via the MarshalledConfig annotation on either the class or method level: // Servlet with transforms applied @Rest( ... ) @MarshalledConfig( calendarFormat=CalendarFormat.ISO_INSTANT, // Calendars serialized/parsed as ISO8601 date-time strings binaryFormat=BinaryFormat.BASE64 // Byte arrays serialized/parsed as BASE64-encoded strings ) public MyResource extends BasicRestServlet {...} Config annotations are defined for all serializers and parsers: MarshalledConfig CsvConfig HtmlConfig HtmlDocConfig JsonConfig JsonSchemaConfig MsgPackConfig OpenApiConfig ParserConfig PlainTextConfig SerializerConfig SoapXmlConfig UonConfig UrlEncodingConfig XmlConfig See Also PetStoreResource.getPetPhoto(long) / putPetPhoto(long,BufferedImage) - A petstore example of REST endpoints that use a custom serializer and parser (PetPhotoSerializer / PetPhotoParser) to upload/serve a pet's photo.

One common security vulnerability is the ability to create arbitrary Java object instances through crafted user input. For example, support for constructing POJOs based on an input attribute defining a fully-qualified class name like {class:'com.foo.MyBean',...} Fortunately, Juneau does not support an open-ended class attribute. As a rule, it should not be possible to create arbitrary POJOs by any of the parsers. The demarshalled object types are inferred via reflection of the class objects passed in through the parser method (e.g. JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(input, MyBean.class)). As long as the Class object passed into this method is not constructed from user-generated input, it should be free from demarshalling vulnerabilities. The following example shows a potential vector that circumvents the restriction above: // Don't do this! Class c = Class.forName(someUserInputString); JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(input, c); // Oops! Security hole! Juneau does support something similar to a class attribute that allows you to define the POJO type at runtime. This is the type attribute. The difference is that it's not possible to specify fully-qualified class names in type attributes, and instead can only specify type keys defined through bean dictionaries. Instead of serializing the fully-qualified class names in the output, we instead serialize type names that represent those POJO types. i.e. instead of class='com.foo.MyBean', we instead serialize type='MyBeanIdentifier'. Since bean types are defined at compile time, it's impossible to instantiate arbitrary POJOs. POJO types of generalized input are also inferred through swaps. Again, since the POJO types are hardcoded at compile time, these should not be subject to demarshalling vulnerabilities. However, it is possible to circumvent this through your swap implementation as shown below: // Don't do this! public class MyInsecureSwap extends ObjectSwap { public Object swap(MarshallingSession session, JsonMap input) throws Exception { // Security hole! return Class.forName(input.getString("class")).newInstance(); } } All other parsers (JSON, URL-Encoding, MessagePack, etc...) work the same way in determining POJO types, so should be safe from demarshalling vulnerabilities.

When assessing the security of any library, its dependent libraries must also be taken into account: The JSON, MessagePack, URL-Encoding, and UON parsers are written from scratch and do not rely on any third-party parsing technology. The XML and HTML parsers use the built-in Java StAX parser (javax.xml.stream), which ships with the JDK. This should be free from vulnerabilities. The RDF parsers (in the separate juneau-marshall-rdf module) rely on Apache Jena. This is the only marshalling code path that pulls in a heavyweight third-party parser; if you do not use RDF, Jena is not on your classpath. No known security vulnerabilities affect the Juneau marshalling code at this time. Vulnerabilities in transitive dependencies (such as Jena) are tracked and remediated per the project's security policy.

Bean Dictionaries — defining type names so POJO types are resolved from a compile-time registry instead of fully-qualified class names. Marshallers — the marshaller API overview. REST Security — denial-of-service mitigation for the REST layer.

Juneau serializers have sophisticated support for transforming relative URIs to absolute form. The following example shows a bean containing URIs of various forms and how they end up serialized. // Our bean with properties containing various kinds of URIs. public class TestURIs { public URI a = URI.create("http://www.apache.org/a"), b = URI.create("/b"), c = URI.create("/c/x/y"), d = URI.create("d"), e = URI.create("e/x/y"), f = URI.create(""), g = URI.create("context:/g/x"), h = URI.create("context:/h"), i = URI.create("context:/"), j = URI.create("context:/.."), k = URI.create("servlet:/k/x"), l = URI.create("servlet:/l"), m = URI.create("servlet:/"), n = URI.create("servlet:/.."), o = URI.create("request:/o/x"), p = URI.create("request:/p"), q = URI.create("request:/"), r = URI.create("request:/.."); } // Create a serializer. WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer .create() .simple() .uriContext( UriContext.of( "http://foo.com:123", // Authority "/myContext", // Context root "/myServlet", // Servlet path "/myPath" // Path info ) ) .uriResolution(ABSOLUTE) .uriRelativity(RESOURCE) .build(); // Produces: // { // a:'http://www.apache.org/a', // b:'http://foo.com:123/b', // c:'http://foo.com:123/c/x/y', // d:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet/d', // e:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet/e/x/y', // f:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet', // g:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/g/x', // h:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/h', // i:'http://foo.com:123/myContext', // j:'http://foo.com:123' // k:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet/k/x', // l:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet/l', // m:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet', // n:'http://foo.com:123/myContext', // o:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet/myPath/o/x', // p:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet/myPath/p', // q:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet/myPath', // r:'http://foo.com:123/myContext/myServlet' // } String json = serializer.write(new TestURIs()); URI resolution is controlled by the following settings: Serializer.BuilderuriContext(UriContext) - Setting that defines the URI contextual information used to resolve relative URIs.uriRelativity(UriRelativity) - Setting that defines how relative URIs should be interpreted. Possible values:UriRelativity.RESOURCE - Relative URIs should be considered relative to the servlet URI. (e.g. http://host:port/context-root/servlet-path).UriRelativity.PATH_INFO - Relative URIs should be considered relative to the request URI. (e.g. http://host:port/context-root/servlet-path/path-info).uriResolution(UriResolution) - Setting that defines the final format of serialized URIs. Possible values:UriResolution.ABSOLUTE - Resolve to an absolute URL. (e.g. http://host:port/context-root/servlet-path/path-info).UriResolution.ROOT_RELATIVE - Resolve to a root-relative URL. (e.g. "/context-root/servlet-path/path-info").UriResolution.NONE - Don't do any URL resolution. Juneau automatically interprets any URL and URI objects as URIs and will resolve them accordingly. The @Uri annotation can be used to extend that to other bean properties and class types so that they also get interpreted as URIs. Example // Applied to a class whose toString() method returns a URI. @Uri public class MyURI { @Override /* Object */ public String toString() { return "http://localhost:9080/foo/bar"; } } // Applied to bean properties public class MyBean { @Uri public String beanUri; @Uri public String getParentUri() { ... } }

RestMatchers are used to allow multiple Java methods to be tied to the same HTTP method and path but differentiated by some request attribute such as a specific header value. Example // GET method that gets invoked for administrators @RestGet(path="/*", matchers=IsAdminMatcher.class) public Object doGetForAdmin() { ... } // GET method that gets invoked for everyone else @RestGet("/*") public Object doGetForEveryoneElse() { ... } The interface for matchers is simple: public class IsAdminMatcher extends RestMatcher { @Override /* RestMatcher */ public boolean matches(RestRequest req) { return req.isUserInRole("ADMINS_GROUP"); } } note If no methods are found with a matching matcher, a 412 Precondition Failed status is returned. If multiple matchers are specified on the same method, ONLY ONE matcher needs to match for the method to be invoked. Note that you CANNOT define identical paths on different methods UNLESS you use matchers. That includes paths that are only different in variable names (e.g. /foo/{bar} and /foo/{baz}). If you try to do so, a ServletException will be thrown on startup. Methods with matchers take precedence over methods without. Otherwise, methods are attempted in the order they appear in the class. See Also RestOpmatchers The following matchers are provided: RestMatcherMultipartFormDataMatcherUrlEncodedFormMatcher

The MemoryStore class is simply an in-memory storage location for configuration files. There is no hard persistence and is used primarily for testing purposes. However, the implementation provides a good idea on how stores work (especially the write method): public class MemoryStore extends ConfigStore { // Some methods ommitted. private final ConcurrentHashMap cache = new ConcurrentHashMap(); @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized String read(String name) { return emptyIfNull(cache.get(name)); } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized String write(String name, String expectedContents, String newContents) { // This is a no-op. if (isEquals(expectedContents, newContents)) return null; String currentContents = read(name); if (expectedContents != null && ! isEquals(currentContents, expectedContents)) return currentContents; update(name, newContents); // Success! return null; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized MemoryStore update(String name, String newContents) { cache.put(name, newContents); super.update(name, newContents); // Trigger any listeners. return this; } }

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from MessagePack using ultra-efficient serializers and parsers. MessagePack is a compact binary form of JSON. The serialization support for MessagePack mirrors that of JSON.

The serializer emits Content-Type: application/msgpack (the RFC 6838-conforming value, matching the constant org.apache.juneau.http.header.ContentType.APPLICATION_MSGPACK). The parser accepts both application/msgpack and the legacy octal/msgpack value as a backward-compatibility alias, so payloads produced by earlier Juneau releases continue to decode without changes.

MessagePack is a FULL-capability streaming format. The MsgPackParser implements TokenReadable and ArrayRecordReadable; the MsgPackSerializer implements TokenWritable and ArrayRecordWritable. This means you can read and write MessagePack using fine-grained structural token cursors in O(1) memory, without materializing the entire document. See Token-Streaming Basics for the full capability matrix and API overview, Token Streaming for the TokenReader/TokenWriter API, and Array-Record Streaming for element-by-element access over top-level arrays (including the writeArrayRecords(output, expectedCount) streaming count overload for MsgPack).

As mentioned previously, the lifecycle methods for the Microservice class are explicitly defined as non-final so that they can be overridden by subclasses. In addition to this support, an interface for defining event listeners for your microservice: Microservice.Builderlistener(MicroserviceListener)MicroserviceListeneronStart(Microservice) onStop(Microservice) onConfigChange(Microservice,ConfigEvents)BasicMicroserviceListener This listener API can be used for listening for and reacting to configuration changes on the file system. public class MyMicroserviceListener extends BasicMicroserviceListener { @Override /* MicroserviceListener */ public void onConfigChange(Microservice microservice, ConfigEvents events) { // Restart the microservice if anything was modified in one of our sections if (events.isSectionChanged("MySection")) microservice.stop().start(); } } Note that the Microservice.onConfigChange(ConfigEvents) method can also be overridden to react to configuration changes as well: public class MyMicroservice extends Microservice { @Override /* MicroserviceListener */ public void onConfigChange(ConfigEvents events) { // Restart the microservice if anything was modified in one of our sections if (events.isSectionChanged("MySection")) this.stop().start(); } }

The Jetty Microservice API consists of a combination of the Juneau Core, Server, and Client APIs and an embedded Eclipse Jetty Servlet Container. The API builds upon the juneau-microservice classes to produce easy-to-create and easy-to-use microservices in a standard Java 17+ environment. Renamed in 9.5 — juneau-microservice-core is now published as juneau-microservice. The Jetty module is no longer a subclass of Microservice; it contributes a single @Configuration class (JettyConfiguration) that the user adds to Microservice.Builder.configurations(...). The juneau-microservice-jetty library consists of the following classes: org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty - PackageJettyMicroservice - Zero-config static-call facade that boots a Jetty microservice in a single line.JettyConfiguration - @Configuration class that wires Jetty into a Microservice.JettyServerComponent - Lifecycle-participating bean that owns the Jetty server.JettySettings - Immutable value bean holding programmatic Jetty knobs (ports, jetty.xml, var resolution).JettyServerFactory - Interface for defining custom Jetty server factories.BasicJettyServerFactory - Default factory that builds the server from jetty.xml.HealthProbeConfiguration - Opt-in @Configuration that auto-mounts the health/readiness/liveness probe servlet. The most-basic creation of a Jetty microservice from an entry-point method is shown below: public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Microservice .create() .args(args) .configurations(JettyConfiguration.class, AppConfig.class) .build() .start() .startConsole() .join(); } @Configuration public static class AppConfig { @Bean Servlet rootResources() { return new RootResources(); } } } RootResources (or any @Bean Servlet whose class is annotated with @Rest) is auto-mounted at the path declared in @Rest(path = "...").

Juneau microservices are self-contained, deployable REST servers built on top of the Juneau REST server framework. A microservice packages your REST resources, configuration, and an embedded HTTP container into a single executable jar (or WAR) that you can start with a plain java -jar command. The microservice layer builds on top of the full Juneau stack: Juneau Microservice Stackjuneau-microservice — core lifecycle, config, console, inject bootstrapjuneau-rest-server — @Rest / @RestOp REST engine (serialization, routing, guards, …)juneau-marshall — multi-format POJO marshalling (JSON, XML, HTML, YAML, …)Deployment target (one of Jetty / Tomcat / Spring Boot)

Juneau provides three independently-releasable deployment adapters. All three share the same Microservice + @Configuration + @Bean Servlet programming model and the same lifecycle contracts. Module When to use juneau-microservice-jetty Default choice for standalone runnable jars. Ships a zero-config JettyMicroservice.run(args, servlet) one-liner and a classpath-driven jetty.xml knob for advanced connector tuning. juneau-microservice-tomcat Drop-in alternative when your organisation standardises on Tomcat, or when you want to share [Tomcat] config between an embedded dev launcher and a full Tomcat deployment. juneau-rest-server-springboot Integration point for Spring Boot applications. REST resources extend BasicSpringRestServlet / BasicSpringRestServletGroup so Spring @Autowired injection and @Bean resolution flow through the Spring application context instead of the Juneau bean store. All three adapters depend on juneau-microservice for the core lifecycle engine and on juneau-rest-server for the REST framework itself.

Every Juneau microservice follows a builder → configure → start → join/stop lifecycle. MicroserviceMicroservice.create() — obtain a fluent builderbuilder.args(args) — pass CLI argumentsbuilder.configurations(…) — register @Configuration classes (adds the HTTP container)builder.build() — construct the Microservice instancestart() — start all MicroserviceListeners (including the HTTP container)startConsole() — (optional) launch interactive stdin consolejoin() — block the calling thread until stop() is calledstop() — stop all listeners in reverse order; close the bean store All methods on Microservice return this, making it easy to chain the whole bootstrap in one fluent expression.

The core lifecycle engine lives in a small, self-contained set of packages and classes: Microservice APIorg.apache.juneau.microservice - Main packageMicroservice - The base microservice class.Microservice.Builder - Builder for the microservice class.MicroserviceListener - Interface for hooking into lifecycle events of the microservice.BasicMicroserviceListener - No-op adapter for the MicroserviceListener interface.org.apache.juneau.microservice.console - Console packageConsoleCommand - Abstract class for defining interactive console commands. By itself the core API provides only the bootstrap machinery — an executable-jar lifecycle, config resolution, command-line-argument and manifest access, an interactive console, and the inject bean store. The embedded HTTP server is contributed by a deployment adapter (Jetty, Tomcat, or Spring Boot) registered as a @Configuration class.

The following is the smallest complete Juneau microservice: a single REST resource mounted on an embedded Jetty server with automatic JSON/XML/HTML content negotiation. Add the dependency: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-microservice-jetty</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> Define a REST resource: import org.apache.juneau.rest.annotation.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; @Rest( path = "/hello", title = "Hello World" ) public class HelloResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet(path = "/*", summary = "Returns a greeting.") public String sayHello() { return "Hello, World!"; } } Boot it from main: import org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty.*; public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { JettyMicroservice.run(args, new HelloResource()).join(); } } JettyMicroservice.run(args, servlet) is a convenience facade that wires JettyConfiguration into the Microservice builder, registers the servlet, starts on port 10000 (or as configured in juneau.cfg), launches the interactive console, and blocks. Point a browser at http://localhost:10000/hello — the default HTML view renders automatically. For the Tomcat or Spring Boot equivalents, see the module-specific pages listed in the Deployment Targets section above.

Every microservice reads its runtime settings from an INI-style juneau.cfg file that is resolved from the classpath or working directory at startup. Key sections used by the built-in modules: [Microservice] # Name and version shown in the console banner. name = MyApp version = 1.0 [Jetty] # Comma-separated list of candidate ports; first available wins. 0 = random. port = 8080, 0 [Logging] # Root logging level (java.util.logging). level = WARNING # Log file relative to the working directory. logFile = logs/microservice.%g.log The configuration is exposed as a Config object through Microservice.getConfig() and is also registered in the bean store so @Bean factory methods can inject it directly.

Config supports file-watch hot-reload out of the box. When the underlying juneau.cfg file changes on disk, listeners registered via Config.addListener(…) are notified with the full set of changed entries. The microservice uses this to propagate logging level changes and port-list updates without a restart. You can register your own listener from a @Configuration class: import org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.*; import org.apache.juneau.config.event.*; import org.apache.juneau.microservice.*; @Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean MicroserviceListener configWatcher() { return new BasicMicroserviceListener() { @Override public void onConfigChange(Microservice ms, ConfigEvents events) { System.out.println("Config changed: " + events); } }; } } The onConfigChange(Microservice, ConfigEvents) callback fires on the calling thread of the file-store watcher, not the request thread, so keep it non-blocking. The ConfigEvents argument carries the full set of changed entries — see Listeners for reacting to specific sections.

The Jetty and Tomcat launchers expose several built-in REST endpoints under the root path when management mixins are enabled. These are opt-in: add the appropriate mixin to your root @Rest resource. Endpoint Mixin / feature Description GET /healthz Health Probes Aggregated health/liveness check. Returns 200 OK or 503 Service Unavailable. GET /readyz Health Probes Readiness probe, used by Kubernetes load-balancer pre-stop hooks. GET /livez Health Probes Liveness probe for pod restart decisions. GET /actuator Management Surface Actuator-style endpoint listing all available management sub-paths. GET /api Auto-generated via Swagger / OpenAPI Swagger 2.x JSON schema; OPTIONS on any resource returns an inline schema. GET /stats Execution Statistics Per-operation call counts, error rates, and latency percentiles. The management surface is implemented via the standard Juneau mixin pack mechanism — there are no special microservice APIs. The same mixins work in a plain servlet container too.

Microservice owns an internal WritableBeanStore populated from every @Configuration class registered on the builder. This makes it easy for companion modules — such as JettyConfiguration and TomcatConfiguration — to contribute lifecycle components and for user code to wire in application services without subclassing. @Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean Servlet rootResources() { return new RootResources(); } // auto-mounted by JettyConfiguration @Bean MyService myService() { return new MyService(); } // available to other @Bean methods } public class App { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Microservice.create() .args(args) .configurations(JettyConfiguration.class, AppConfig.class) .build() .start() .startConsole() .join(); } } JettyConfiguration walks the bean store at startup, finds every @Bean whose declared return type is Servlet and whose runtime class carries @Rest, and mounts it at the path declared in @Rest(path = "..."). TomcatConfiguration follows an identical contract. See Inject-Aware Microservice for a complete reference on resolution priority, @PostConstruct / @PreDestroy callbacks, and external bean store integration.

Apache Juneau provides three minimal clone-and-go starter projects — one per deployment target — that demonstrate a HelloResource, content negotiation, a Swagger/OPTIONS page, @Path/@Query binding, a YAML config file, and a MockRestClient test: Starter Deployment Links Jetty Embedded Jetty, runnable jar GitHub · Docs Spring Boot Spring Boot, runnable jar GitHub · Docs Tomcat WAR on Tomcat 10+ GitHub · Docs See Starter Projects for full details.
