The following tables are the complete reference for how each POJO datatype is rendered by XmlSerializer. They mirror how the same data structures are represented in JSON. See XML Methodology for a conceptual overview of the mapping rules.

Loose maps and beans use the element <object> for encapsulation. _type attributes are added to bean properties or map entries if the type cannot be inferred through reflection (e.g. an Object or superclass/interface value type). Data type JSON example XML Map { k1: 'v1', k2: null } <object> <k1>v1</k1> <k2 _type='null'/> </object> Map { k1: 123, k2: 1.23, k3: null } <object> <k1>123</k1> <k2>1.23</k2> <k3 _type='null'/> </object> Map { k1: 'v1', k2: 123, k3: 1.23, k4: true, k5: null } <object> <k1>v1</k1> <k2 _type='number'>123</k2> <k3 _type='number'>1.23</k3> <k4 _type='boolean'>true</k4> <k5 _type='null'/> </object>

Loose collections and arrays use the element <array> for encapsulation. Collections (e.g. List, Set) serialize identically to their array equivalents. Data type JSON example XML String[] ['foo', null] <array> <string>foo</string> <null/> </array> Number[] [123, 1.23, null] <array> <number>123</number> <number>1.23</number> <null/> </array> Object[] ['foo', 123, 1.23, true, null] <array> <string>foo</string> <number>123</number> <number>1.23</number> <boolean>true</boolean> <null/> </array> String[][] [['foo', null], null] <array> <array> <string>foo</string> <null/> </array> <null/> </array> int[] [123] <array> <number>123</number> </array> boolean[] [true] <array> <boolean>true</boolean> </array> List<String> ['foo', null] <array> <string>foo</string> <null/> </array> List<Number> [123, 1.23, null] <array> <number>123</number> <number>1.23</number> <null/> </array> List<Object> ['foo', 123, 1.23, true, null] <array> <string>foo</string> <number>123</number> <number>1.23</number> <boolean>true</boolean> <null/> </array>

Data type JSON example XML class MyBean { public String a; public int b; public Object c; // String value public Object d; // Integer value public MyBean2 e; public String[] f; public int[] g; } class MyBean2 { String h; } { a: 'foo', b: 123, c: 'bar', d: 456, e: { h: 'baz' }, f: ['qux'], g: [789] }
Data type JSON example XML class MyBean { public Map a; public Map b; public Map c; } { a: { k1: 'foo' }, b: { k2: 123 }, c: { k3: 'bar', k4: 456, k5: true, k6: null } }

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from XML using ultra-efficient serializers and parsers. The XML serializer converts POJOs directly to XML without the need for intermediate DOM objects. Likewise, the XML parser uses a STaX parser and creates POJOs directly without intermediate DOM objects. Unlike frameworks such as JAXB, Juneau does not require POJO classes to be annotated to produce and consume XML. However, several XML annotations are provided for handling namespaces and fine-tuning the format of the XML produced. The following example shows XML for a typical bean:

@Marshalled(typeName="person") public class Person { // Bean properties public String name; @MarshalledProp(calendarFormat=CalendarFormat.ISO_INSTANT) public Calendar birthDate; public List addresses; // Getters/setters omitted } @Marshalled(typeName="address") public class Address { // Bean properties public String street, city; public StateEnum state; public int zip; public boolean isCurrent; // Getters/setters omitted }

Person person = new Person() .name("John Smith") .birthDate("1946-08-12T00:00:00Z") .addresses( new Address() .street("100 Main Street") .city("Anywhereville") .state(NY) .zip(12345) .isCurrent(true) );

<person> <name>John Smith</name> <birthDate>1946-08-12T04:00:00Z</birthDate> <addresses> <address> <street>100 Main Street</street> <city>Anywhereville</city> <state>NY</state> <zip>12345</zip> <isCurrent>true</isCurrent> </address> </addresses> </person> Juneau produces JSON-equivalent XML, meaning any valid JSON document can be losslessly converted into an XML equivalent. In fact, all of the Juneau serializers and parsers are built upon this JSON-equivalence.
The @YamlConfig annotation is used to apply YAML serializer and parser configuration annotations to REST resources, methods, and other contexts.

YAML support can be added to REST resources using the BasicYamlConfig interface or by including the YAML serializer and parser in BasicUniversalConfig: // YAML-only REST resource @Rest public class MyYamlResource extends RestServlet implements BasicYamlConfig { @RestGet("/person/{id}") public Person getPerson(@Path int id) { return findPerson(id); } } // Universal resource supporting JSON, XML, HTML, UON, and YAML @Rest public class MyUniversalResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { @RestGet("/person/{id}") public Person getPerson(@Path int id) { return findPerson(id); } }

You can configure the YAML serializer and parser through annotation or programmatic builders: @Rest( serializers = YamlSerializer.class, parsers = YamlParser.class, defaultAccept = "application/yaml" ) public class MyResource extends RestServlet { ... }
juneau-config now supports YAML config files as an alternative to INI/CFG files.

Use a .yml or .yaml config name to auto-select YAML format: Config c = Config.create() .name("MyConfig.yaml") .build(); You can also force YAML explicitly: Config c = Config.create() .name("MyConfig.cfg") .yaml() .build();
INI section paths map directly to nested YAML maps: [foo/bar/baz] k1 = v1 foo: bar: baz: k1: v1 A config lookup like config.getString("foo/bar/baz/k1") works the same for either format.
INI remains the default format. FileStore now searches cfg,yml,yaml by default. Existing value modifiers and SVL variable resolution continue to work unchanged.

The YAML data type produced depends on the Java object type being serialized. Primitives and primitive objects are converted to YAML scalars. Beans and Maps are converted to YAML block mappings. Collections and arrays are converted to YAML block sequences. Anything else is converted to YAML string scalars (with quoting if necessary).

POJO type YAML type Example Serialized form String Scalar serialize("foobar"); foobar Number Scalar serialize(123); 123 Boolean Scalar serialize(true); true Null Scalar serialize(null); null Beans with properties of any type on this list Block mapping serialize(new MyBean()); p1: val1
p2: true Maps with values of any type on this list Block mapping serialize(new TreeMap()); key1: val1
key2: true Collections and arrays of any type on this list Block sequence serialize(new Object[]{1,"foo",true}); - 1
- foo
- true Date/time types (Calendar, Date, Temporal subtypes, Duration) are serialized natively as ISO 8601 strings. Swaps can be used to convert non-serializable POJOs into serializable forms (such as byte[] arrays to Base-64 encoded strings) or to override the default format for types that already have built-in support.

YAML strings are quoted when they contain special characters or could be misinterpreted: Strings that are YAML reserved words (null, true, false, yes, no, etc.) are double-quoted. Strings that look like numbers are double-quoted. Strings containing special YAML characters (:, #, {, }, [LINKLABEL_0], etc.) are double-quoted. Strings with leading or trailing whitespace are double-quoted. Empty strings are double-quoted. Strings containing control characters (\n, \t, \b, etc.) are double-quoted with proper escape sequences.

YAML uses indentation to represent nested structures. Each level of nesting increases the indent by 2 spaces: person: name: John Smith addresses: - street: 100 Main Street city: Anywhereville state: NY - street: 200 Oak Avenue city: Sometown state: CA Empty maps and collections are serialized using flow-style notation ({} and [] respectively).

The YamlParser class is used to parse YAML into POJOs. The class hierarchy for the builder of this parser is: Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderParser.BuilderReaderParser.BuilderYamlParser.Builder Refer to the builder javadocs for configurable settings. The following pre-configured parsers are provided for convenience: YamlParserDEFAULT The YAML parser supports: Block-style mappings and sequences (indentation-based). Flow-style mappings ({key: value}) and sequences ([item1, item2]). Plain, single-quoted, and double-quoted scalars. Literal block scalars (|) and folded block scalars (>). Comments (# ...). Null values (null, ~). Booleans (true, false). Integer and floating-point numbers. Document markers (---, ...). Bean type dictionaries via _type property.

// Parse YAML into a POJO MyBean bean = YamlParser.DEFAULT.read(yaml, MyBean.class); // Parse into generic types JsonMap map = YamlParser.DEFAULT.read(yaml, JsonMap.class); JsonList list = YamlParser.DEFAULT.read(yaml, JsonList.class); // Parse with generic type parameters List<MyBean> beans = YamlParser.DEFAULT.read(yaml, List.class, MyBean.class); // Use the Yaml marshaller for convenience MyBean bean = Yaml.to(yaml, MyBean.class);

The YamlSerializer class is used to serialize POJOs into YAML. The class hierarchy for the builder of this serializer is: Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderMarshallingTraverseContext.BuilderSerializer.BuilderWriterSerializer.BuilderYamlSerializer.Builder Refer to the builder javadocs for configurable settings. The following pre-configured serializers are provided for convenience: YamlSerializerDEFAULTDEFAULT_READABLE

// Serialize a POJO to YAML String yaml = YamlSerializer.DEFAULT.write(myBean); // Create a custom serializer YamlSerializer s = YamlSerializer.create() .addBeanTypes() .trimNullProperties() .build(); String yaml = s.write(myBean); // Use the Yaml marshaller for convenience String yaml = Yaml.of(myBean);

The YAML serializer produces block-style output by default. Beans and maps are formatted with each property on its own line, and collections/arrays use the YAML block sequence marker (-). The DEFAULT_READABLE variant produces the same output as DEFAULT since YAML is inherently human-readable through its indentation-based format.

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from YAML using native serializers and parsers implemented without any external dependencies. The YAML serializer converts POJOs directly to YAML block-style output using indentation-based structure. The YAML parser creates POJOs directly from YAML using an indentation-aware state machine. The following example shows YAML for a typical bean:

public class Person { // Bean properties public String name; @MarshalledProp(calendarFormat=CalendarFormat.ISO_INSTANT) public Calendar birthDate; public List addresses; // Getters/setters omitted } public class Address { // Bean properties public String street, city; public StateEnum state; public int zip; public boolean isCurrent; // Getters/setters omitted }

Person person = new Person() .name("John Smith") .birthDate("1946-08-12T00:00:00Z") .addresses( new Address() .street("100 Main Street") .city("Anywhereville") .state(NY) .zip(12345) .isCurrent(true) );
name: John Smith birthDate: '1946-08-12T00:00:00Z' addresses: - street: 100 Main Street city: Anywhereville state: NY zip: 12345 isCurrent: true
// Use the default serializer to serialize a POJO to YAML String yaml = YamlSerializer.DEFAULT.write(someObject); // Use the marshaller for convenience String yaml = Yaml.of(someObject);
// Use the default parser to parse YAML into a POJO MyBean bean = YamlParser.DEFAULT.read(yaml, MyBean.class); // Use the marshaller for convenience MyBean bean = Yaml.to(yaml, MyBean.class);
Produces: application/yaml Accepts: application/yaml, text/yaml

The parser supports: Block-style mappings and sequences Flow-style mappings ({key: value}) and sequences ([item1, item2]) Plain, single-quoted, and double-quoted scalars Literal block scalars (|) and folded block scalars (>) Comments (# ...) Null values (null, ~) Booleans (true, false) Integer and floating-point numbers Document markers (---, ...) Bean type dictionaries via _type property

// Use BasicYamlConfig for YAML-only REST resources @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicYamlConfig { ... } // YAML is also included in BasicUniversalConfig @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... } See Also YAML Methodology for data type conversion details. Security Analysis Apache Juneau takes security seriously and uses automated tools to help identify potential security vulnerabilities and code quality issues. Current Security Status​ Analysis Results​ GitHub CodeQL Analysis → - Security vulnerability detection SonarCloud Quality Analysis → - Code quality, security, and maintainability About Our Analysis Tools​ GitHub CodeQL​ We use GitHub CodeQL for automated security analysis. CodeQL is GitHub's semantic code analysis engine that helps identify: Security vulnerabilities - Potential security issues in your code Bugs and errors - Logic errors and potential runtime issues Code quality issues - Patterns that could lead to problems SonarCloud​ We use SonarCloud for comprehensive code quality analysis. SonarCloud provides: Code quality metrics - Maintainability, reliability, and security ratings Technical debt analysis - Time to fix code quality issues Code coverage integration - Test coverage analysis with JaCoCo Security hotspot detection - Potential security vulnerabilities Code smell detection - Anti-patterns and maintainability issues Duplication analysis - Code duplication detection Analysis Schedule​ Our security and quality analysis runs automatically: CodeQL: Every Thursday at 3:15 AM UTC SonarCloud: Every Monday at 2:00 AM UTC On every push to the master branch On every pull request to the master branch Languages analyzed: Java Security Reporting​ If you discover a security vulnerability in Apache Juneau, please report it responsibly: For Critical Security Issues​ Do not report critical security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues.
